title: Why Washington, D.C. Isn't a State: The 10-Mile Square
summary: The Constitution lets Congress rule a federal district of up to ten miles square, which is why Washington, D.C. has more people than Wyoming or Vermont but no voting member of Congress. Here is how the district got its shape, and the main arguments for and against statehood, from both sides' own sources.
sources: US Constitution, Article I, Section 8, Clause 17 (District Clause): Congress shall have power 'To exercise exclusive Legislation in all Cases whatsoever, over such District (not exceeding ten Miles square) as may, by Cession of particular States, and the Acceptance of Congress, become the Seat of the Government' (Constitution Annotated): https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/article-1/section-8/clause-17

US Constitution, Article I, Sections 2-3: the House is composed of Members chosen by the People of the several States; the Senate of two Senators from each State (National Archives transcript): https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/constitution-transcript

US Constitution, 23rd Amendment: the District appoints electors equal to the number of Senators and Representatives it would have if a State, 'but in no event more than the least populous State' (Constitution Annotated): https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/amendment-23/twenty-third-amendment-historical-background

Congressional Research Service, R47101, DC Statehood: Constitutional Considerations for Proposed Legislation (12 May 2022): Federalist No. 43 on 'the indispensable necessity of complete authority at the seat of government'; ten miles square is 100 square miles; on 9 Jul 1846 Congress retroceded the Virginia portion on the assent of Alexandria's voters; the House passed H.R. 51 in June 2020, the first time either house passed such a bill; H.R. 51 would admit 'Washington, Douglass Commonwealth' and keep the White House, the Capitol and nearby federal buildings as the seat of government; Congress retains plenary legislative authority over the District; arguments that Maryland's consent is required, and the reply that no part of the District is in Maryland's jurisdiction; the 23rd Amendment as a separate consideration; retrocession to Maryland as an alternative: https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R47101.html

City of Alexandria, Alexandria African American History Trail, Retrocession: President Polk signed the retrocession in July 1846; Alexandria's port had been eclipsed by Baltimore and New York; slaveholders feared abolitionists would succeed in the District: https://www.alexandriava.gov/sites/default/files/2023-12/AAHT-3-Retrocession.pdf

US Census Bureau, 2020 Census resident population (table reproduced by the Maryland Department of Planning): District of Columbia 689,545; Vermont 643,077; Wyoming 576,851: https://planning.maryland.gov/MSDC/Documents/Census/Census2020/resident-population.pdf
Office of the Clerk, US House, Roll Call 132, 22 Apr 2021, H.R. 51 Washington, D.C. Admission Act, On Passage: Yeas 216, Nays 208: https://clerk.house.gov/evs/2021/roll132

DC Office of Statehood (Government of the District of Columbia), Why Statehood: DC elects a non-voting Delegate who 'can draft legislation but cannot vote'; DC residents 'pay more per capita to the federal government than any state'; 'Congress interferes with our local laws': https://statehood.dc.gov/page/why-statehood-dc

Senate Republican Policy Committee, Practical and Legal Problems with D.C. Statehood (19 Apr 2021): 'a constitutional amendment would be required'; 'The first family would effectively get three electoral votes'; 'Joe Biden received 93% of the vote in D.C.': https://www.rpc.senate.gov/policy-papers/practical-and-legal-problems-with-dc-statehood
Derived: Wyoming has 3 voting members of Congress (2 senators + 1 representative), equal to its 3 electoral votes as the least populous state (23rd Amendment; Senate RPC)

Map data: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com and US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (public domain) https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/carto-boundary-file.html; the ten-mile square, the Potomac, the 1846 line and the federal core are drawn schematically

scenes.narration: More people live in Washington, D.C. than in Wyoming, or in Vermont.
Yet Wyoming has {3|three} voting members of Congress. D.C. has {0|zero}: just a House delegate who can't vote.

data.title: More people, *no vote*
data.source: US Constitution; DC Office of Statehood

scenes.narration: So why isn't the nation's capital a state? The answer is in the Constitution, and the two sides read it very differently.
By the end, you'll know why the Founders built it this way, and the strongest case on each side today.
The Constitution lets Congress take a district, up to ten miles square, from the states, as the seat of government.

data.source: US Constitution, Art. I, Sec. 8, Cl. 17

scenes.narration: Over that district, Congress holds exclusive legislation in all cases whatsoever. Not a governor. Not a state.
Why? James Madison wrote of the indispensable necessity of complete authority at the seat of government.
The land came from Maryland and Virginia: a square of {100|a hundred} square miles, across the Potomac River.
In {1846|eighteen forty-six}, Congress handed the Virginia side back. Alexandria's port was fading, and slaveholders feared the capital would end slavery.
That's why today's D.C. is a square with one side cut away by the river.
If you like maps that explain things, subscribe. There's a new map every other day.

The case for statehood starts with people. The {2020|twenty twenty} census counted {689,545|six hundred eighty-nine thousand} in D.C., {643,077|six hundred forty-three thousand} in Vermont, and {576,851|five hundred seventy-seven thousand} in Wyoming.
D.C.'s government says its residents pay more federal tax per person than people in any state.

data.source: DC Office of Statehood, Why Statehood

scenes.narration: And Congress can overrule its local laws. Congress's own researchers call its power over D.C. plenary: total.
In {2020|twenty twenty}, the House passed a statehood bill for the first time. In {2021|twenty twenty-one}, it passed again, {216|two hundred sixteen} to {208|two hundred eight}.

data.source: Office of the Clerk, Roll Call 132 (2021); CRS R47101

scenes.narration: The bill would shrink the federal district to its core, around the White House and the Capitol. The rest would become a state: Washington, Douglass Commonwealth.
Opponents read the same Constitution and see a different answer.
The Senate Republican Policy Committee argues that making D.C. a state would take a constitutional amendment, not just a law.
Some say Maryland must agree, because the land was once Maryland's. Supporters answer that no part of D.C. is in Maryland today.
Then there's the {23rd|twenty-third} Amendment, which gives the district {3|three} electoral votes. Shrink the district, critics say, and the first family would effectively get them.
Another idea: give the homes back to Maryland, the way the Virginia side went back in {1846|eighteen forty-six}.
Politics hangs over all of it. In {2020|twenty twenty}, D.C. gave Joe Biden {93%|ninety-three percent} of its vote.

scenes.chapter: So why isn't it a state?
scenes.narration: So D.C. isn't a state because the Constitution made it Congress's district, and every bill to change that has stopped short of becoming law.
Until that changes, more people than Wyoming or Vermont live in a place the Constitution calls a district, not a state.
There's a new map every other day. Pick one, and I'll see you there.
